title: 'Hollow Lacedaemon, full of ravines'
greek: κοίλην Λακεδαίμονα κητώεσσαν (koilēn Lakedaimona kētōessan)
short: Lacedaemon is the district around Sparta in the deep Eurotas valley; the epithet kētōessa was already obscure in antiquity ('full of clefts' or 'vast').
body: The line repeats Iliad 2.581. Merry and Riddell, following Buttmann, take Lacedaemon as the name of the district whose chief town is Sparta, and koilē ('hollow') as describing the valley between the Taygetus and Parnon ranges, quoting the geographer Tozer. For kētōessa they derive the word from kētos in the sense 'gulf, hollow', and so 'cavernous, full of rifts', citing Strabo's report that the fissures caused by Laconia's earthquakes were called kaietoi and Zenodotus' reading kaietaessan. Strabo also records the sense 'great', which he thought more plausible. Merry and Riddell conclude that the epithet refers to the many rifts in the ground. Murray's 'with its many ravines' follows this view.

title: The double wedding at Sparta
greek: τὸν δ᾽ εὗρον δαινύντα γάμον πολλοῖσιν ἔτῃσιν υἱέος ἠδὲ θυγατρὸς (ton d' heuron dainunta gamon polloisin etēisin huieos ēde thugatros)
short: Telemachus arrives during a double wedding: Hermione goes to Achilles' son Neoptolemus, and Megapenthes, Menelaus' son by a slave woman, takes a Spartan bride.
body: Menelaus had promised Hermione to Neoptolemus at Troy; the wedding binds the house of Atreus to Achilles' line. Megapenthes' name means 'Great Grief', perhaps recalling Menelaus' sorrow at Helen's loss; Helen had no more children after Hermione. Merry and Riddell discuss tēlugetos, applied to Megapenthes, and doubt that it means 'late-born'. A minstrel sings and two tumblers (kubistētēre) whirl among the dancers; these lines (4.17-19) closely resemble the dance on the shield of Achilles (Iliad 18.604-606). Merry and Riddell report from Athenaeus (5.180) that Diodorus, a follower of Aristophanes of Byzantium, struck out the whole wedding, and that some modern critics treat lines 3-19 as an interpolation, but they observe that removing them leaves an awkward join. The festivity contrasts sharply with the stalled marriage question in Ithaca.

title: Menelaus rebukes Eteoneus: the duty of hospitality
greek: οὐ μὲν νήπιος ἦσθα, Βοηθοΐδη Ἐτεωνεῦ, τὸ πρίν … ἦ μὲν δὴ νῶι ξεινήια πολλὰ φαγόντε (ou men nēpios ēstha, Boēthoidē Eteōneu, to prin … ē men dē nōi xeinēia polla phagonte)
short: When his squire asks whether to admit the strangers, Menelaus calls him a fool: he and Helen often ate other men's hospitality on their way home.
body: Eteoneus' question is reasonable, since the house is busy with a wedding, but it breaks the rule that a stranger at the gate must be received. Menelaus' answer grounds the rule in reciprocity: 'we two ate full often hospitable cheer of other men' (xeinēia, gifts or meals of hospitality). The reception follows the standard sequence also seen in Ithaca and Pylos: horses stabled, guests led in, bathed by maids, anointed, clothed, seated, given water for their hands and a meal; questions come only afterwards (4.60-62). Steve Reece and M. W. Edwards have analysed this sequence as a type-scene. Menelaus even gives them the 'fat ox-chine' that was his own portion of honour (4.65-66).

anchor: gleam as of sun or moon
title: Menelaus' palace: bronze, gold, electrum, silver and ivory
greek: ὥς τε γὰρ ἠελίου αἴγλη πέλεν ἠὲ σελήνης … χρυσοῦ τ᾽ ἠλέκτρου τε καὶ ἀργύρου ἠδ᾽ ἐλέφαντος (hōs te gar ēeliou aiglē pelen ēe selēnēs … chrusou t' ēlektrou te kai argurou ēd' elephantos)
short: The young men gaze at a palace that shines 'as of sun or moon'; Telemachus whispers that Zeus' court must look like this.
body: The same line describes the palace of Alcinous (7.84), and Merry and Riddell explain its compressed syntax. Telemachus lists the flashing of 'bronze, gold, electrum, silver and ivory' (4.71-73). Electrum is either a natural alloy of gold and silver, as Pliny understood it, explicitly citing this passage, or amber. Merry and Riddell note that standing between gold and silver it seems to be the metal, but that in the two other Homeric passages (15.460, 18.295) it must be amber beads on a necklace. Menelaus overhears and answers modestly: no mortal can rival Zeus, and his wealth came at the cost of his brother's murder and years of wandering (4.78-99). The wealth of Sparta is thus shadowed from the start.

anchor: Libya, where the lambs are horned
title: Menelaus' wanderings: Cyprus, Phoenicia, the Erembi and Libya
greek: Αἰθίοπάς θ᾽ ἱκόμην καὶ Σιδονίους καὶ Ἐρεμβοὺς καὶ Λιβύην, ἵνα τ᾽ ἄρνες ἄφαρ κεραοὶ τελέθουσι (Aithiopas th' hikomēn kai Sidonious kai Eremboús kai Libuēn, hina t' arnes aphar keraoi telethousi)
short: Menelaus' eight years of travel take him to the Sidonians, the mysterious Erembi, and Libya, where lambs are born horned and ewes lamb three times a year.
body: The list reflects Greek knowledge of the Levant and North Africa. Merry and Riddell note that the Sidonians are distinguished from the Phoenicians, as in Iliad 23.740-744, and that the Erembi are named only here; Strabo already debated whether they were cave-dwellers, Arabs (Zeno emended to 'Arabs'), or, as Posidonius suggested, 'Arambi' (perhaps Aramaeans). Libya's lambs 'horned at once' were quoted by Herodotus (4.29) and Aristotle; Merry and Riddell prefer the sense 'born horned'. The triple lambing and endless milk belong to the poem's interest in fabulous abundance at the edges of the world, comparable to the Cyclopes' unploughed fields. Menelaus gathered 'much livelihood' on these travels, a frank picture of wealth won by voyaging and gift-getting.

title: Telemachus weeps behind his cloak
greek: χλαῖναν πορφυρέην ἄντ᾽ ὀφθαλμοῖιν ἀνασχών (chlainan porphureēn ant' ophthalmoiin anaschōn)
short: At the mention of his father Telemachus hides his tears behind his cloak; Menelaus notices and guesses who he is.
body: The gesture is the first step in a recognition scene. Menelaus debates whether to let the youth speak or to question him (4.117-119), and Helen's entrance settles the matter: she recognizes Telemachus at once by his likeness to his father (4.138-146). The same gesture recurs famously with Odysseus himself at the Phaeacian court, where he covers his head with his purple cloak to hide his tears at Demodocus' songs of Troy and Alcinous alone notices (8.83-92, 8.521-534). The parallel links father and son and shows how song and memory provoke grief in the poem. Sheila Murnaghan's study of disguise and recognition places these scenes in the poem's larger pattern.

anchor: like Artemis of the golden arrows
title: Helen 'like Artemis of the golden arrows'
greek: ἤλυθεν Ἀρτέμιδι χρυσηλακάτῳ ἐικυῖα (ēluthen Artemidi chrusēlakatōi eikuia)
short: Helen enters like the goddess Artemis; the epithet chrysēlakatos can mean 'of the golden arrow' or 'of the golden distaff', and Helen, appropriately, carries a distaff.
body: Ēlakatē usually means 'distaff', and Helen is about to be handed a golden distaff and a silver wool-basket (4.131-135). Merry and Riddell argue that with Artemis the epithet must mean 'with golden arrows', since in the Iliad it is joined with 'shooter of arrows' (Iliad 20.70-71), and that the scholia record both senses of ēlakatē; but they also suggest a visual point in the comparison: a distaff, like an arrow, is a long straight rod, so that Helen, distaff in hand, could be taken for Artemis with her shaft. The simile presents Helen as a domestic queen of almost divine dignity, at odds with her own self-reproach a few lines later. Nausicaa is also compared to Artemis (6.102-109).

title: Egyptian Thebes and Helen's gifts
greek: ὃς ἔναι᾽ ἐνὶ Θήβῃς Αἰγυπτίῃς, ὅθι πλεῖστα δόμοις ἐν κτήματα κεῖται (hos enai' eni Thēbēis Aiguptiēis, hothi pleista domois en ktēmata keitai)
short: Helen's silver work-basket on wheels was a gift from Alcandre, wife of Polybus of Egyptian Thebes, the richest city in the world.
body: Egyptian Thebes (Luxor/Karnak), capital of the New Kingdom pharaohs, was proverbial for wealth; Achilles names it as the richest place he can think of, with its hundred gates (Iliad 9.381-384). Merry and Riddell record that Greek Thēbē renders an Egyptian popular name for the city. Polybus gave Menelaus two silver baths, two tripods and ten talents of gold, and his wife gave Helen a golden distaff and a silver basket 'with wheels beneath', which Merry and Riddell, following Apollonius and Hesychius, explain as 'on castors', comparing the wheeled tripods Hephaestus makes in Iliad 18.373-377. The gifts show the Mycenaean world's real links with Egypt and the poem's fascination with exotic luxury.

title: 'For the sake of shameless me' (kunōpis)
greek: ὅτ᾽ ἐμεῖο κυνώπιδος εἵνεκ᾽ Ἀχαιοὶ ἤλθεθ᾽ ὑπὸ Τροίην (hot' emeio kunōpidos heinek' Achaioi ēlthet' hupo Troiēn)
short: Helen calls herself kunōpis, literally 'dog-eyed' or 'dog-faced': a harsh word for shamelessness, which she uses of herself in the Iliad too.
body: The dog in Homer is a byword for shamelessness and greed. Helen calls herself 'dog' and 'dog-faced' in her self-reproaches in the Iliad (3.180, 6.344, 6.356), and Achilles calls Agamemnon 'dog-eyed' (Iliad 1.159, 1.225). Her readiness to blame herself publicly is part of her complex characterization: she is honoured and gracious in Sparta, yet she reminds her guests that the war was fought for her. Later in the scene she blames Aphrodite for her 'blindness' (atē, 4.261-264). Scholars such as Linda Clader and Norman Austin have explored how Homer manages Helen's double image as both cause of the war and self-aware narrator of it.

title: Peisistratus' tears for Antilochus; mourning customs
greek: τόν ῥ᾽ Ἠοῦς ἔκτεινε φαεινῆς ἀγλαὸς υἱός … κείρασθαί τε κόμην βαλέειν τ᾽ ἀπὸ δάκρυ παρειῶν (ton rh' Ēous ekteine phaeinēs aglaos huios … keirasthai te komēn balein t' apo dakru pareiōn)
short: All weep, and Peisistratus thinks of his brother Antilochus, killed by Memnon, 'the glorious son of the bright Dawn'; he then politely asks to postpone weeping until morning.
body: Memnon, king of the eastern Ethiopians and son of Eos, killed Antilochus at Troy; Merry and Riddell note that Achilles then killed Memnon in revenge, a story told in the Cyclic Aethiopis and by Pindar (Pythian 6.28-42). Peisistratus' speech is a model of tact: he does not object to grief, for 'this is the only due we pay to miserable mortals, to cut the hair and let a tear fall from the cheeks' (4.197-198), but he takes 'no joy in weeping at supper time'. Merry and Riddell compare the cutting of hair for the dead in Iliad 23.46 and 23.135 and Odyssey 24.46. Menelaus praises his good sense as worthy of his father.

anchor: spins the thread of good fortune
title: Zeus 'spins the thread' of fortune
greek: ᾧ τε Κρονίων ὄλβον ἐπικλώσῃ γαμέοντί τε γεινομένῳ τε (hōi te Kroniōn olbon epiklōsēi gameonti te geinomenōi te)
short: Menelaus says Zeus 'spins' good fortune for a man at marriage and birth: the image of fate as spun thread.
body: The verb epiklōthein, 'to spin to someone', gives the metaphor of fate as a thread allotted at birth, which in Hesiod and later becomes the work of the three Moirai, Clotho ('Spinner'), Lachesis and Atropos (Theogony 904-906). Homer uses the image of the gods 'spinning' destinies several times (1.17, 3.208, 20.196; Iliad 24.525). Merry and Riddell discuss the order 'at marriage and at birth', a reversal they explain partly by metre and partly by Menelaus' thought moving from Nestor's happy marriage back to his good fortune from birth. Nestor is the example: a sleek old age at home and wise, valiant sons, the opposite of Menelaus' troubled house and Odysseus' lost years.

title: Helen's drug (nēpenthes) from Egypt
greek: φάρμακον … νηπενθές τ᾽ ἄχολόν τε, κακῶν ἐπίληθον ἁπάντων (pharmakon … nēpenthes t' acholon te, kakōn epilēthon hapantōn)
short: Helen mixes into the wine an Egyptian drug that banishes grief and anger and brings forgetfulness of every ill, given her by Polydamna, wife of Thon.
body: Nēpenthes means 'griefless' (nē-, 'not', + penthos, 'grief'). Merry and Riddell note that Homer's mention of the earth suggests a plant and that the verb 'cast' suggests a solid. Candidates proposed include opium, henbane and the borage that Dioscorides says cheers when put in wine; Plutarch and Macrobius instead allegorized the drug as Helen's charming eloquence. Thon's name, they observe, recalls a town Thonis near Canopus (Strabo; compare Herodotus 2.113-115). Diodorus later used the passage to argue that Homer had visited Egypt, claiming that women of Egyptian Thebes still used such a drug (1.97.7). Homer says Egyptians are all physicians, 'of the race of Paeeon', the gods' healer (Iliad 5.401, 5.899-901). Anne Bergren and others have read the drug as a figure for Helen's storytelling, which follows at once.

anchor: in the fashion of a slave
title: Helen's tale: Odysseus enters Troy as a beggar
greek: αὐτόν μιν πληγῇσιν ἀεικελίῃσι δαμάσσας, σπεῖρα κάκ᾽ ἀμφ᾽ ὤμοισι βαλών, οἰκῆι ἐοικώς (auton min plēgēisin aeikeliēisi damassas, speira kak' amph' ōmoisi balōn, oikēi eoikōs)
short: Helen tells how Odysseus disfigured himself, dressed in rags and slipped into Troy as a beggar-slave; only she recognized him, bathed him, and kept his secret.
body: The story anticipates the second half of the poem, where Odysseus returns to his own house disguised as a beggar, is bathed by a woman who recognizes him (Eurycleia, Book 19), and kills his enemies. Helen presents herself as already loyal to the Greeks: when Odysseus killed many Trojans, 'my soul was glad, for already my heart was turned to go back to my home'. She blames Aphrodite for the 'blindness' (atē) that led her away. Merry and Riddell comment on the reflexive use of auton min, 'himself', in 4.244. The episode was told also in the Cyclic Little Iliad. Its self-serving slant is answered by Menelaus' story that follows.

title: Menelaus' tale: Helen at the Wooden Horse
greek: ἵππῳ ἔνι ξεστῷ, ἵν᾽ ἐνήμεθα πάντες ἄριστοι Ἀργείων (hippōi eni xestōi, hin' enēmetha pantes aristoi Argeiōn)
short: Menelaus answers with a story of Helen at the Wooden Horse, imitating the Greek wives' voices; only Odysseus' restraint saved the men inside.
body: Helen, followed by her new Trojan husband Deiphobus, three times circled 'the hollow ambush', calling the chieftains by name in their wives' voices. Diomedes and Menelaus wanted to answer, but Odysseus held them back and clamped his hands over the mouth of Anticlus. Merry and Riddell report that Aristarchus rejected lines 285-289 and that the scholia say Anticlus came 'from the Cycle'; they find some force in the objections. The two stories, told one after the other, sit uneasily together: Helen's shows her as a secret ally, Menelaus' as a dangerous seducer who nearly destroyed the Greeks. Critics such as Anne Bergren and S. D. Olson read the pair as a muted marital quarrel conducted through praise of Odysseus. Odysseus himself asks Demodocus to sing the Horse in Book 8 (8.492-520).

title: The deer in the lion's lair
greek: ὡς δ᾽ ὁπότ᾽ ἐν ξυλόχῳ ἔλαφος κρατεροῖο λέοντος νεβροὺς κοιμήσασα νεηγενέας γαλαθηνοὺς (hōs d' hopot' en xulochōi elaphos krateroio leontos nebrous koimēsasa nēgeneas galathēnous …)
short: Menelaus pictures the suitors as fawns laid by a doe in a lion's den: when the lion returns he will kill them, a forecast of the slaughter in Book 22.
body: Merry and Riddell note how many points correspond: the thicket stands for Odysseus' house, the fawns (and perhaps the doe) for the suitors, the lion for Odysseus, and the lion's absence and return for his wandering and homecoming. The whole simile is repeated by Telemachus to Penelope at 17.124-131, linking the beginning and the end of the plot. Lion similes are common in the Iliad's battle scenes; in the Odyssey they are fewer and more pointed. Later in this book the image is turned around: Penelope, worrying for her son, is compared to a lion surrounded by hunters in a closing ring (4.791-793), so that the predator becomes the trapped animal. Menelaus also wishes Odysseus might come with the strength he showed in a wrestling match against Philomeleides on Lesbos (4.341-344).

title: Proteus, 'the unerring old man of the sea'
greek: γέρων ἅλιος νημερτὴς ἀθάνατος Πρωτεὺς Αἰγύπτιος, ὅς τε θαλάσσης πάσης βένθεα οἶδε, Ποσειδάωνος ὑποδμώς (gerōn halios nēmertēs athanatos Prōteus Aiguptios …)
short: Proteus is an immortal sea god of Egypt, Poseidon's servant, who knows all the depths of the sea and tells the truth (nēmertēs) only when caught and held.
body: His name suggests prōtos, 'first', and the 'old man of the sea' is a type shared with Nereus and Phorcys. He is called 'unerring' because, once mastered, he speaks without deceit, and like Atlas he 'knows the depths of every sea' (compare 1.52-53). Herodotus (2.112-120) turned him into a historical king of Memphis who kept Helen in Egypt while the Greeks fought at Troy for a phantom, a version going back to Stesichorus' Palinode and dramatized in Euripides' Helen, where he appears as a dead king and his daughter is called Theonoe. Proteus' prophecy gives Menelaus three pieces of news (Ajax, Agamemnon, Odysseus) and his own destiny, Elysium. His shape-changing made 'protean' an English word.

title: Pharos, the island off Egypt
greek: νῆσος ἔπειτά τις ἔστι πολυκλύστῳ ἐνὶ πόντῳ Αἰγύπτου προπάροιθε, Φάρον δέ ἑ κικλήσκουσι (nēsos epeita tis esti poluklustōi eni pontōi Aiguptou proparoithe, Pharon de he kiklēskousi)
short: Menelaus is becalmed for twenty days on Pharos, which he puts a day's sail from Egypt, though the real Pharos lay just off the later Alexandria.
body: The island became famous for the lighthouse built there under the Ptolemies, joined to Alexandria by a mole. Homer's distance ('as far as a hollow ship runs in a whole day') puzzled ancient readers. Strabo discusses it, suggesting either Homer's limited knowledge of Egypt or the change of coastline caused by the Nile's silt; Herodotus had already called Egypt 'the gift of the river' (2.5). 'Aegyptus' in Homer is the name of the river as well as the land (4.477). The detail that the men fished with hooks because hunger pinched them (4.368-369) is notable: Homeric heroes normally eat meat, and fishing is a sign of need, as with Odysseus' crews on Thrinacia (12.329-332).

title: Eidothea and the stratagem of the seal-skins
greek: Εἰδοθέη … φῶκαι νέποδες καλῆς ἁλοσύδνης … ἀμβροσίην ὑπὸ ῥῖνα ἑκάστῳ θῆκε (Eidothea … phōkai nepodes kalēs halosudnēs … ambrosiēn hupo rhina hekastōi thēke)
short: Proteus' daughter pities Menelaus and teaches him to hide under fresh seal-skins among the herd; she puts ambrosia under each man's nose to kill the stench.
body: Merry and Riddell note that Eidothea was called Theonoe in later tradition and that her name may refer either to her father's 'forms' (eidos) or to his knowledge (eidenai). The seals are 'the brood (nepodes) of the fair Halosydne'; they discuss whether nepodes means 'web-footed', 'footless' or 'offspring', and prefer 'brood', and they treat halosydnē, 'sea-born', as a descriptive title rather than a proper name. The episode mixes the grotesque with the divine: the fishy stench is countered with ambrosia, the gods' immortal substance, which Merry and Riddell explain as food or ointment that sustains immortality. A daughter betraying her father's secret to help a stranger is a folk-tale motif.

title: Proteus' transformations
greek: λέων γένετ᾽ ἠυγένειος, αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα δράκων καὶ πάρδαλις ἠδὲ μέγας σῦς· γίγνετο δ᾽ ὑγρὸν ὕδωρ καὶ δένδρεον ὑψιπέτηλον (leōn genet' ēugeneios, autar epeita drakōn kai pardalis ēde megas sus …)
short: Seized, Proteus becomes a lion, a serpent, a leopard, a boar, running water and a tall tree, but the men hold on until he tires and answers.
body: Eidothea had warned that he would take the shape 'of all things that move upon the earth, and of water, and of wondrous blazing fire' (4.417-418). The motif of wrestling with a shape-changing sea god to force a prophecy or a marriage recurs in Greek myth: Peleus wins Thetis by holding her through her changes (Pindar, Nemean 4.62-65), and Heracles wrestles Nereus to learn the way to the Hesperides (Apollodorus 2.5.11). Virgil imitates the whole episode in Aristaeus' capture of Proteus (Georgics 4.387-452). Merry and Riddell question the usual rendering of ēugeneios as 'bearded' and suggest it may simply mean 'noble'. Allegorical readers from antiquity onward made Proteus a figure for matter or for the changing forms of nature.

title: Aegyptus, 'the heaven-fed river' (the Nile)
greek: Αἰγύπτοιο, διιπετέος ποταμοῖο (Aiguptoio, diipeteos potamoio)
short: In Homer the Nile is called Aegyptus, the same name as the land; diipetēs, 'fallen from Zeus', means fed by rain.
body: Merry and Riddell explain diipetēs as 'fallen from Zeus', that is, rain-fed, and note Eustathius' remark that the epithet suits the Nile because its flood comes from heavy summer rains in Ethiopia, as Aristotle and Eudoxus held. The same epithet is used of other rivers (Spercheios, Iliad 16.174) and Strabo argues that Homer applies it to rivers in general. The name Neilos first appears in Hesiod (Theogony 338). Proteus tells Menelaus that he must sail back up to the river and offer proper hecatombs before the gods will let him go home; the failure to sacrifice, not any great crime, has held him. Menelaus does so and raises a cenotaph to Agamemnon there (4.581-584).

title: The death of the Locrian Ajax
greek: Αἴας μὲν μετὰ νηυσὶ δάμη δολιχηρέτμοισι. Γυρῇσίν μιν πρῶτα Ποσειδάων ἐπέλασσεν (Aias men meta nēusi damē dolichēretmoisi. Gurēisin min prōta Poseidaōn epelassen)
short: Ajax son of Oileus, hated by Athena, is saved from shipwreck, boasts he escaped despite the gods, and is drowned when Poseidon splits the rock he clings to.
body: This is the 'lesser' Ajax of Locris, not the Telamonian Ajax of 3.109. Merry and Riddell note that Athena's anger arose from his outrage on Cassandra and that Virgil follows the story (Aeneid 1.39-45); here, however, his death is caused by his insolence against the gods. They discuss the location of the Gyraean rocks, placed near Myconos by some ancient scholars and, more plausibly, off Caphereus, the south-eastern cape of Euboea, by Quintus of Smyrna; Euripides' Trojan Women (lines 87-94) has Poseidon promise to strew those coasts with the dead. The story is a pointed example of the theme of Book 1: men suffer through their own reckless folly, here a boast against the gods.

title: Agamemnon slain 'as one slays an ox at the stall'
greek: τὸν δ᾽ οὐκ εἰδότ᾽ ὄλεθρον ἀνήγαγε καὶ κατέπεφνε δειπνίσσας, ὥς τίς τε κατέκτανε βοῦν ἐπὶ φάτνῃ (ton d' ouk eidot' olethron anēgage kai katepephne deipnissas, hōs tis te katektane boun epi phatnēi)
short: Proteus tells how Aegisthus set a watchman, laid an ambush of twenty men, feasted Agamemnon and killed him like an ox at the manger.
body: In this version Aegisthus, not Clytemnestra, is the killer, and the murder happens at a banquet, a perversion of hospitality. Merry and Riddell compare Iliad 17.61 for the syntax and note the gnomic aorist. The simile of the ox at the stall is used again by Agamemnon's ghost (11.409-411), where Clytemnestra's part is stressed. The details sharpen the parallel with Ithaca: a host's feast becomes a slaughter, an ambush of twenty men awaits a returning prince (compare Antinous' plan at 4.669-672), and the hall is filled with corpses. Agamemnon's tearful kiss of his native soil on landing (4.521-523) makes his death more pathetic, and anticipates Odysseus' own landing in Book 13. Aeschylus' Agamemnon gives the classic tragic version, with Clytemnestra the killer in the bath.

title: The Elysian plain
greek: ἐς Ἠλύσιον πεδίον καὶ πείρατα γαίης … ὅθι ξανθὸς Ῥαδάμανθυς (es Ēlusion pedion kai peirata gaiēs … hothi xanthos Rhadamanthus)
short: Menelaus will not die but be sent to the Elysian plain at the world's end, where life is easiest, because as Helen's husband he is Zeus' son-in-law.
body: Merry and Riddell describe Elysium as a place for chosen heroes not in Hades but on the surface of the earth in the far west, where they live with their bodies, not as shades. The climate is perfect: no snow, storm or rain, only the cooling west wind sent up by Ocean. Rhadamanthus, son of Zeus and brother of Minos (Iliad 14.321-322), dwells there. Hesiod speaks of the 'Islands of the Blessed' for the race of heroes (Works and Days 167-173) and Pindar of the island of the blessed (Olympian 2.68-80). The privilege comes not from Menelaus' virtue but from his marriage, a frank statement of the logic of divine favour. The contrast with Achilles' bleak view of death (11.488-491) is striking. The etymology of Ēlusion is unknown; Merry and Riddell record guesses including 'the place where men go'.

title: Ithaca, 'a pasture-land of goats'
greek: ἐν δ᾽ Ἰθάκῃ οὔτ᾽ ἂρ δρόμοι εὐρέες οὔτε τι λειμών· αἰγίβοτος, καὶ μᾶλλον ἐπήρατος ἱπποβότοιο (en d' Ithakēi out' ar dromoi eurees oute ti leimōn; aigibotos, kai mallon epēratos hippobotoio)
short: Telemachus politely declines Menelaus' gift of horses: rocky Ithaca has no broad courses or meadows, but he loves it more than horse-pasturing land.
body: The reply shows Telemachus' growing tact and his attachment to home. Ithaca is 'goat-pasturing' (aigibotos), and 'not one of the islands that lean upon the sea is fit for driving horses'. Merry and Riddell quote Horace's adaptation of the passage in a letter where he refuses a patron's gift: Ithaca 'is not a place suited to horses, neither stretched out in level spaces nor lavish with grass' (Epistles 1.7.40-43). Menelaus smiles, strokes him, and praises his good blood; he exchanges the gift for a silver mixing-bowl made by Hephaestus. The description of Ithaca's rough terrain has been used in the debate over whether Homer's Ithaca is the modern island.

title: The silver mixing-bowl, 'the work of Hephaestus'
greek: δώσω τοι κρητῆρα τετυγμένον … ἔργον δ᾽ Ἡφαίστοιο. πόρεν δέ ἑ Φαίδιμος ἥρως, Σιδονίων βασιλεύς (dōsō toi krētēra tetugmenon … ergon d' Hēphaistoio. poren de he Phaidimos hērōs, Sidoniōn basileus)
short: Menelaus gives Telemachus his finest treasure, a silver krater with gilded rim, made by Hephaestus and given to him by Phaedimus, king of the Sidonians.
body: Treasures in Homer carry histories: who made them, who gave them, and on what occasion. A krater is the large bowl in which wine was mixed with water. 'Work of Hephaestus' may mean literally divine workmanship or simply supreme craftsmanship. Sidonian silverwork was famous: the prize bowl in the funeral games for Patroclus was a Sidonian krater that Phoenicians brought across the sea (Iliad 23.740-749). Gift-exchange between guest-friends binds them in obligation, as M. I. Finley stressed. The gift is actually handed over when Telemachus leaves Sparta (15.113-129), where the same lines recur and Helen adds a robe for his future bride.

title: The suitors' ambush
greek: ὄφρα μιν αὐτὸν ἰόντα λοχήσομαι ἠδὲ φυλάξω ἐν πορθμῷ Ἰθάκης τε Σάμοιό τε παιπαλοέσσης (ophra min auton ionta lochēsomai ēde phulaxō en porthmōi Ithakēs te Samoio te paipaloessēs)
short: Learning from Noemon that Telemachus has really sailed, Antinous plans to ambush him with twenty men in the strait between Ithaca and Samos.
body: The scene shifts back to Ithaca, where the suitors are throwing the discus and javelin 'in insolence of heart' (hubris). Noemon's innocent request for his ship reveals Telemachus' voyage, and his remark that he saw Mentor, 'or a god', going aboard, though Mentor was still in Ithaca, hints at Athena's hand. Antinous' plan to murder the prince marks the suitors' move from wasting property to attempted murder, which justifies the final vengeance. The twenty-man ambush repeats Aegisthus' ambush of Agamemnon (4.530-531). The plot is left hanging at the end of the book, with the suitors waiting at Asteris, and the poem turns to Odysseus in Book 5; it is resolved when Telemachus evades them on Athena's advice (15.27-42, 16.342-370).

title: 'Her knees were loosened': Penelope's grief
greek: τῆς δ᾽ αὐτοῦ λύτο γούνατα καὶ φίλον ἦτορ … αἵ θ᾽ ἁλὸς ἵπποι ἀνδράσι γίγνονται (tēs d' autou luto gounata kai philon ētor … hai th' halos hippoi andrasi gignontai)
short: Hearing of the plot, Penelope's 'knees and heart were loosened', a formula for shock or collapse; she calls ships 'horses of the sea' and sinks down on the threshold.
body: 'His knees were loosened' is used in Homer both of death in battle and of overwhelming emotion; here it marks the shock of the news. Penelope asks why her son needed to board ships, 'which serve men as horses of the deep', a vivid kenning-like metaphor; Merry and Riddell note that hippoi here means chariots, team and car together, and compare Aeschylus' 'chariots of sailors' for ships (Prometheus Bound 468). Unable to sit on a chair, she sits on the threshold of her chamber lamenting, surrounded by her maids. Her lament (4.722-741) echoes that of Book 1 and shows her as isolated and uninformed: even her nurse had kept the secret. She sends for Dolius, the servant her father gave her, to tell Laertes.

title: Penelope's prayer to Athena
greek: κλῦθί μευ, αἰγιόχοιο Διὸς τέκος, Ἀτρυτώνη (kluthi meu, aigiochoio Dios tekos, Atrutōnē)
short: Bathed and in clean clothes, Penelope puts barley grains in a basket, prays to Athena 'Atrytone' (the unwearied) to save her son, and raises the ritual cry; the goddess hears.
body: Atrutōnē is an old title of Athena, usually explained as 'unwearied' or 'untiring', from a- ('not') and truō ('wear out'), though its formation is uncertain. Penelope follows Eurycleia's advice: purification by bathing and fresh clothes (compare Telemachus' washing at 2.261), the offering of barley, and an appeal to past sacrifices ('If ever Odysseus ... burnt to thee fat thigh-pieces'), the 'remember if ever' form of Greek prayer found as early as Chryses' prayer in Iliad 1.39-41. She ends with the ololygē, the women's ritual cry that also marked Nestor's sacrifice (3.450). Merry and Riddell, on 3.450, cite this line as an example of the joyful religious cry.

title: The phantom of Iphthime and the 'gates of dreams'
greek: εἴδωλον ποίησε, δέμας δ᾽ ἤικτο γυναικί, Ἰφθίμῃ … ἡδὺ μάλα κνώσσουσ᾽ ἐν ὀνειρείῃσι πύλῃσιν (eidōlon poiēse, demas d' ēikto gunaiki, Iphthimēi … hēdu mala knōssous' en oneireiēisi pulēisin)
short: As Penelope sleeps, Athena sends a phantom in the form of her sister Iphthime to reassure her about Telemachus; it will not say whether Odysseus lives.
body: Penelope is first compared to a lion encircled by hunters (4.791-793), then sleep takes her. The dream-figure enters 'by the thong of the bolt' and stands over her head, the standard posture of Homeric dream visitors (compare the dream sent to Agamemnon, Iliad 2.20). It speaks of 'the gods that live at ease' (rheia zōontes), a formula for divine ease contrasted with human suffering. Penelope sleeps 'at the gates of dreams'; Merry and Riddell refer to her later speech on the two gates of dreams, of horn for true dreams and ivory for false (19.560-569), which Virgil adapted at the end of Aeneid 6. The phantom's refusal to speak of Odysseus, 'an ill thing to speak words vain as wind', keeps suspense alive as the book ends.

title: Asteris, the islet of the ambush
greek: Ἀστερίς, οὐ μεγάλη· λιμένες δ᾽ ἔνι ναύλοχοι αὐτῇ ἀμφίδυμοι (Asteris, ou megalē; limenes d' eni naulochoi autēi amphidumoi)
short: A rocky islet 'midway between Ithaca and rugged Samos' with a double harbour, where the suitors lie in wait: its identification is a key problem of Homeric geography.
body: Strabo, citing Apollodorus, reported that the islet in the strait between Ithaca and Cephallenia (ancient Samos or Same) did not have the harbours Homer describes, and that changes in the land might explain the difference. The usual candidate today is Daskalio, a tiny rock in the Ithaca channel, which has no real harbour. The difficulty is part of the wider debate about Homer's Ithaca and its neighbours (Dulichium, Same, Zacynthus, 1.246), on which Merry and Riddell write an appendix, and which led Dörpfeld to put Ithaca on Leucas and Bittlestone more recently on the Paliki peninsula of Cephallenia. The book ends here, with the ambush in place: the Telemachy's plot is suspended while the poem turns to Odysseus himself.
